name: Erik Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager on the Harland Estate, 600 hectares owned by the Harland family. We run 250 outdoor sows, about 2,000 pigs at any time, and grow potatoes and wheat. I start at half six walking the sow paddocks, then it's the potato store, the lads, and the phone ringing all day. I've been there 24 years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good bit is that I know every field by its smell after rain, and old Mr Harland trusts me completely. What grinds me down is that he's 80 now and his son Rupert is taking over. Rupert reads farming magazines on his tablet and wants drones and sensors in everything, and I've never used any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would suit me. I've never touched those AI things and I don't see what they'd add to a pig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the market that the clever stuff turned out to be mostly talk, which is what I thought. I wouldn't gloat, I'd just say it and move on to the price of feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still have Rupert to deal with. AI or not, he wants to change things, and he's talked about selling the potato side to cut staff costs. That worry was there before any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the estate as I do. I'd keep putting money aside with Rosa, as we have been, and I'd try to get on Rupert's good side by showing him the numbers on paper. I'm not going to start using a tablet at 58.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, because of Rupert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly are you worried Rupert might do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell the potato side and cut two of the lads, maybe me down to three days. Old Mr Harland (his employer) shook my hand on this job, and his son Rupert would rather shake hands with a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If that happened, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's plenty of farm work round here, and we've savings. I'd be fine, really. It's the pride I'd mind.

I'd **not gloat**, just move on to the price of feed.
think: I'd still face **Rupert**, who wants to change things anyway.
He's talked of **selling the potato side** to cut staff.
do: Keep running the estate **as I do now**.
Keep **saving** with Rosa as we have been.
Show Rupert the **numbers on paper**, not on a tablet.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, because of Rupert rather than AI.

fieldNote: His standing worry is **the owner's son**, Rupert, not technology.
He fears losing **pride** more than income, given his savings.
He refuses outright to **use a tablet**.

steps.text: Keep running the sow paddocks and potato store as now
Keep putting money aside with his wife Rosa

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side going to computers. Rupert would love that. I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the market that a farm still needs a manager who knows the ground. I'd say it calmly, because getting angry gets you nowhere with owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Rupert would use it as an excuse. The ordering, the pig movement forms and the planning could go to software, and he'd say he only needs a stockman, not a manager. My hands-on work would stay, but my title and pay might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and make myself useful in the yard, where the computer can't go. I'd ask my daughter Nadia, who's an accountant, to check whether Rosa and I could manage on less. And I'd maybe let the office lady use the software, as long as I don't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit more than before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rupert if he cut your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rupert Harland, the estate owner's son, that his software has never smelled a sick pig and never will. Then I'd probably go home and sulk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving to another farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, there's plenty nearby. But I've been at the estate 24 years. You don't just walk off.

feel: He feels **more uneasy** than in the first picture.

fieldNote: About **a fifth** of his week is planning and forms that software could take.

steps.text: Spend more time in the sow paddocks where software can't go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for robots. I'd be 63. That's the one that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast and somebody should slow it down. I'd say it at the market and probably at the parish meeting, though I'm not one for meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished at the estate. Rupert would run the planning on AI from 2028 and buy robots for the sow paddocks in 2031. I'd be 63, with one skill a machine can suddenly do, and I'd lie awake on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Rosa and Nadia this winter and work out if we can stop at 63. I'd put more into savings each month and cancel the new car we were looking at. I wouldn't learn the robots, I'd just plan my exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like being told the date your dog's going to die.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lie awake. Even with savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The money's there, but it's not just money. Twenty-four years on the Harland Estate (the farm he manages), and my last job would be showing a robot where the sows like to farrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else on the estate would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas, who's 40 with three kids. He drives the potato harvester. He'd be gone too, and he hasn't got what Rosa and I have put by.

I'd raise it at the **parish meeting**, though I avoid meetings.
think: I'd be **finished** at the estate by 2031.

feel: He feels **bad**, like knowing the date his dog will die.

fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** at 63 once robots arrive in **2031**.
Thinking AI in **2028** lets Rupert run the planning without him first.
Savings cover him, but the loss of **identity** keeps him awake.

steps.text: Work out with his wife and daughter if they can stop at 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. I'd be 66. I'd planned to stop at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some years, so the government and the owners should use them to look after older workers. I'd say that at the market, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably just make it. My worry is 2031, when the AI does the planning and Rupert decides he doesn't need a manager. But the pigs would still need me until the robots came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold on to my job and keep saving. I'd tell Rupert I plan to retire at 65, so he doesn't push me out early. And I'd keep an eye on jobs at the farms nearby, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see the end of the road from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why tell Rupert your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then he can wait. If Rupert Harland (the owner's son) knows I'm going at sixty-five, he won't spend money pushing me out at sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on doing up the kitchen until I know. Rosa won't like that, but she'll understand.

I'd say it at the market, **quietly**.
think: I'd probably **just make it** to retirement at 65 on the estate.

Keep saving and hold off on the **kitchen refit**.
Watch **jobs at nearby farms**, just in case.
feel: He feels **worried**, but he can see the end of the road.
S3.quote: If Rupert Harland (the owner's son) knows I'm going at sixty-five, he won't spend money pushing me out at sixty-three.
fieldNote: Thinking AI in **2031** could cut his manager role before robots in 2034.

He still holds back on **spending** to stay safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be long gone from the estate by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for people to sort it out, and I wouldn't say much more. It's not my battle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still have Rupert, though. AI or not, he'll change things. But with that much time, I'd retire at 65 on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the estate my way until 65, keep saving, and leave. I wouldn't learn any of the new stuff. Somebody younger can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, still a bit uneasy because of Rupert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your time after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fish, help my son Samir when he's back from the army, and grow the best potatoes in the village. Small ones, for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any advice for younger workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young farm workers should learn the machines I never bothered with, because I had the luck of being born early.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to sort it out.
I'd add that it's **not my battle** any more.
think: **Rupert** would still change things, AI or not.
With that much time, I'd retire at 65 on **my own terms**.
feel: He feels mostly **relieved**, with **lingering unease** about Rupert.
S4.quote: Young farm workers should learn the machines I never bothered with, because I had the luck of being born early.
fieldNote: The decade lets him **retire on time**, before any robots.
His standing worry, **Rupert**, stays in every picture.
He admits he was **lucky with timing**, not prepared.

steps.text: Run the estate his way until 65, then retire

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd be pushed out at 63 by a robot Rupert bought. What would help is a rule that older workers get a proper notice period and a payout when a machine replaces them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the knowledge. When I go, nobody on the Harland Estate (the farm he manages) will know which field floods in February, and no robot is going to ask me.

headlineQuote: When I go, nobody on the Harland Estate (the farm he manages) will know which field floods in February, and no robot is going to ask me.
portrait: Erik is a **58-year-old farm manager** on the privately owned Harland Estate, with pigs and potatoes.
He has worked there **24 years** and never uses AI or tablets.
His standing worry is **Rupert**, the owner's son, who wants to modernise and cut staff.
AGI by 2028 leaves him **alarmed**, expecting to be pushed out at 63.
Longer warning lets him **retire at 65** on his own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he expects to be **pushed out at 63**.
whatWouldHelp: A rule giving older workers a **proper notice period** and a **payout** when machines replace them.
